**Latest arXiv Papers on AI Agent Evaluation (3 most recent)**  

- **DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?**  
  Existing evaluations of AI models on high‑finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real PE and IB work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. The authors introduce DeepFinance, a 21‑task benchmark taking humans an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room of ~19 files and is graded against ~84 expert‑written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. Evaluating 22 model configurations, the best (GPT‑6 Astra with max reasoning) satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision‑relevant evidence without acting on it.  
  [arXiv:2611.10926v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10926v1)  

- **Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems**  
  Agentic AI systems extend LLMs with tools, memory, retrieval, browser/computer‑use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi‑agent coordination. These capabilities create new attack paths: untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. The paper presents a systematic review of 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 attack‑safeguard relationships, organized into eight causal‑mechanism classes. Tool, MCP, and action‑layer attacks dominate, while prompt‑injection and action‑hijacking have the broadest coverage. Safeguard coverage is uneven (only 278 of 660 relationships directly assessed). The analysis supports lifecycle‑aware threat modeling and agent evaluation.  
  [arXiv:2611.10843v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10843v1)  

- **The Devil Wears Markdown: Detecting Malicious Intent Hidden in AI Agent Skill Instructions through Hybrid Static, Dynamic, and Agentic Analysis**  
  Agentic AI ecosystems rely on reusable agent skills that combine executable code, natural‑language instructions, configuration artifacts, and external tool integrations, creating software‑supply‑chain risks. The authors evaluate three open‑source scanners on 140 skills (80 malicious, 60 benign). The default Cisco configuration achieves recall 0.91 with 33 false positives; the LLM‑enabled configuration (Qwen3:8B) achieves recall 0.85 with 40 false positives. They propose a hybrid framework combining static findings, safety‑constrained sandbox evidence, and LLM‑based reasoning. Adding dynamic evidence to skill‑content reasoning raises F1 from 0.70 to 0.85; combining static and dynamic evidence raises F1 to 0.89 (5 false positives). The Full Pipeline detects 68/80 malicious skills, achieving 0.88 accuracy, 0.93 precision, 0.85 recall.  
  [arXiv:2611.10830v1](http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10830v1)

items.title: DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
items.summary: Existing evaluations of AI models on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real private equity (PE) and investment banking (IB) work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. We introduce DeepFinance, an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end PE and IB tasks that take a human professional an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files and is graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. We evaluate 22 model configurations, each in its native agent harness. The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.

items.title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
items.summary: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, retrieval, browser or computer-use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi-agent coordination. Although these capabilities enable agents to act beyond text generation and perform tasks, they also create attack paths through which adversaries can exploit untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. Such attacks can manipulate planning and tool use, corrupt memory, abuse code-execution environments, and trigger harmful downstream effects. In this paper, we present a systematic review of malicious attacks targeting agentic AI systems. We screened 186 candidate sources and retained 98. Following independent coding and resolver adjudication, we identified 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 explicit attack--safeguard relationships. We organize attacks into eight causal-mechanism classes while retaining insertion points, activation conditions, abused capabilities, objectives, impacts, persistence, and evidence as orthogonal dimensions. Our analysis shows that tool, MCP, and action-layer attacks account for the largest share of atomic attacks, while the prompt-injection and action-hijacking class has the broadest paper coverage. We identify distinct class-specific activation patterns and separation between insertion and later activation. Safeguard coverage remains uneven: only 278 of 660 relationships are directly assessed, and strong coverage is uncommon. These findings support lifecycle-aware threat modeling, agent evaluation, tool governance, and defense-in-depth security for agentic AI systems.

items.title: The Devil Wears Markdown: Detecting Malicious Intent Hidden in AI Agent Skill Instructions through Hybrid Static, Dynamic, and Agentic Analysis
items.summary: Agentic AI ecosystems increasingly rely on reusable agent skills that combine executable code, natural-language instructions, configuration artifacts, and external tool integrations. These hybrid artifacts create software supply-chain risks because malicious intent may be distributed across instructions, code, metadata, and runtime behavior, making isolated alerts difficult to interpret. We evaluate three open-source scanners on a held-out test set of 140 skills comprising 80 malicious and 60 benign samples, including Cisco Skill Scanner with and without its optional LLM analyzer. items.title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
